subject: velvet worm
title: This Worm Fires Glue From Its Face, Then Drinks Its Own Weapon

scenes.text: This worm has two cannons on its face. They fire glue.
The velvet worm looks harmless: soft, slow, a few inches long. Then a cricket walks past.
Two nozzles whip side to side up to sixty times a second, spraying twin jets of slime at eleven miles an hour, half a meter out.
scenes.keywords: velvet worm slime jet close up

scenes.text: The slime hardens almost the instant it lands. The cricket is glued to the ground, legs locked.
The worm walks over, injects digestive juices and eats. But first it slurps up its own slime. Protein is too valuable to waste.
It has hunted this way for about 300 million years. Glue cannons, built before the dinosaurs.

description:
The velvet worm hunts by firing two jets of slime from nozzles on its head. High-speed video shows the nozzles oscillating 30 to 60 times a second and the jets leaving at 3 to 5 meters per second, reaching about half a meter.
The slime sets almost immediately into a stiff gel that pins the prey; the worm then injects digestive enzymes, eats the victim and swallows its own slime to recycle the protein. The lineage has barely changed in around 300 million years.
Would you rather face a velvet worm or a spider? Comment below.
first_comment: The slime is about 90 percent water and only 3 to 5 percent protein, yet it sets in an instant. Engineers are copying it for new adhesives. Which animal weapon should we cover next?
